analysis.investment_thesis: Bajaj Electricals is a legacy consumer electricals brand with near-zero revenue growth (0.6% CAGR over 9 years) and declining net profit trends, making it fundamentally incompatible with Fisher's growth investing framework. A P/E of 120x for a business generating INR 133 Cr net profit on INR 4,826 Cr revenue is a value trap, not a growth opportunity.
key_strengths: Strong promoter holding at 62.7% signals long-term owner-operator alignment
OCF positive all 5 years with FCF of INR 318 Cr in FY25 — real cash generation
Debt dramatically reduced from INR 1,084 Cr (2020) to INR 215 Cr (2025), cleaning up the balance sheet
key_risks: Revenue flatline: INR 4,590 Cr (2016) → INR 4,826 Cr (2025), a 0.6% CAGR — this is not a growth company
Operating margin turned negative (-2.10%) while P/E is 120x — profitability is deteriorating, not improving
Intense competition from Havells, Crompton, V-Guard with no evident innovation moat or R&D pipeline
red_flags: P/E of 120x is completely unjustifiable — net profit of INR 133 Cr on INR 4,826 Cr revenue is a ~2.8% net margin
ROE of 7.12% is less than one-third of Fisher's 20%+ threshold — capital is being destroyed in real terms
Net profit trend is contracting (last 5Y) with FY24–FY25 stagnating at ~INR 131–133 Cr despite revenue recovery
Operating income volatile and erratic over 9 years — no consistent margin expansion story
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From my scuttlebutt perspective, Bajaj Electricals is a well-known brand with deep distribution in India — the kind of company that *sounds* like it should be a compounder. But the numbers tell a different story entirely. Revenue has been essentially flat for nearly a decade, net profit peaked at INR 216 Cr in FY23 and has since stagnated around INR 130–133 Cr, and the operating margin has turned negative. When I look for companies worth holding forever, I demand that they be continuously developing new products, expanding margins, and growing earnings at 20%+ annually. Bajaj Electricals fails every one of those tests.

The valuation is the final disqualifier. Paying 120x trailing earnings — and even 28.75x forward earnings — for a business that has compounded revenue at 0.6% and net profit at 2.3% over nine years requires a leap of faith I am unwilling to make. A great company at a fair price beats a fair company at a great price, but this is a stagnant company at an expensive price. The FCF generation (~INR 318 Cr) and balance sheet cleanup are genuine positives, but they do not compensate for the absence of the one thing I care about most: durable, compounding growth driven by innovation and market expansion. I would pass entirely.
